title: Plotting a price series
objectives: Plot prices against dates with a readable date axis.
Draw the daily returns of a price series as a histogram.

widget.solution:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from datetime import date

def plot_prices(days, closes):
    # days are text such as "2024-03-01"
    dates = [date.fromisoformat(d) for d in days]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot(dates, closes)
    ax.set_ylabel("Close (£)")
    fig.autofmt_xdate()
    return ax

hints.text: Every string in `days` needs the same conversion.
A list comprehension applies `date.fromisoformat` to each string.
Write `dates = [date.fromisoformat(d) for d in days]`.

feedback.correct: Real dates on the x axis.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. The x values on the line should be `date` objects, one per string.

byKey.test-1: Nothing was drawn, or the code stopped. Make `dates` a list with one date per string.
byKey.test-2: The x values are still text. Convert each string with `date.fromisoformat`.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. `dates = ...` must become a list of dates.

explain.text:
`date.fromisoformat` reads the year, month and day from each string. matplotlib then places each point by the calendar and picks a few readable ticks. `fig.autofmt_xdate()` tilts the labels so they do not collide.

```python
dates = [date.fromisoformat(d) for d in days]
```

A colleague skips the conversion for a year of 250 closes.

```python

```

matplotlib draws the line without an error.

state.caption: With text, matplotlib does not know these are dates

screens.question: How many tick labels does the x axis get?

options.text: 250: one per string, printed on top of each other

options.why: That is what real dates get. Text is treated as labels, and every label gets a tick.
Text carries no calendar to matplotlib, so it cannot group by month.

options.text: None: the axis is left blank
options.why: matplotlib labels text categories, every one of them.

hints.text: To matplotlib, `"2024-03-01"` is just a word.
Words are treated as categories, like the names on a bar chart.
Each category gets its own tick and label, so 250 strings give 250 labels.

feedback.correct: 250 labels in a black smear along the bottom.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. How does matplotlib treat text on an axis?

byKey.few: You expected a date axis. Strings are categories, and every category gets a labelled tick.
byKey.twelve: Text has no calendar for matplotlib, so it cannot know which strings share a month.

explain.text: Strings become categories, placed one step apart with a label each: 250 overlapping labels. Weekends vanish too, since the gaps are not known. Convert with `date.fromisoformat` and the axis becomes a calendar again.

canvas.caption: Strings: 250 labels. Dates: a few, chosen by matplotlib

screens.title: Choosing the date format
screens.prose:
You can choose how dates are written on the ticks.

```python
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%d %b"))
```

`%d` is the day of the month and `%b` the short month name.
screens.question: What does the tick for 8 March 2024 read?

options.why: `%d` pads to two digits and `%b` is the short month name. `%B` would give March.
The formatter replaces the default style. The pattern has no year.
The pattern puts the day first, so the tick does too.

hints.text: Read the pattern left to right: `%d`, a space, then `%b`.
`%d` is a two-digit day; `%b` is a three-letter month.
8 March becomes `08` then `Mar`: 08 Mar.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply `%d` and `%b` in the order the pattern gives.

byKey.long: `%d` keeps the leading zero, and `%b` is short: 08 Mar. `%-d %B` would be nearer 8 March.

explain.text: `DateFormatter("%d %b")` writes each tick as day then short month: 08 Mar. For a year of data `%b %Y` (Mar 2024) reads better. The codes are the ones `strftime` uses.

widget.solution:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def returns_hist(closes):
    # today / yesterday - 1, for each pair of days
    returns = [b / a - 1 for a, b in zip(closes, closes[1:])]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.hist(returns, bins=20)  # a histogram of returns with 20 bins
    ax.set_xlabel("Daily return")
    ax.set_ylabel("Days")
    return ax
